more: How Roman numerals work

Seven letters carry the values I = 1, V = 5, X = 10, L = 50, C = 100, D = 500 and M = 1,000. Letters are normally written from largest to smallest and added up: MDCLXVI = 1,666. To avoid four identical letters in a row, a smaller letter placed before a larger one is subtracted. Only six such pairs are standard: IV (4), IX (9), XL (40), XC (90), CD (400) and CM (900). That is why 1994 is MCMXCIV – M + CM + XC + IV – rather than MDCCCCLXXXXIIII.
Standard and non-standard forms

You will sometimes see IIII on clock faces or XIIX on old documents. Historically the Romans were flexible, but modern usage follows the strict subtractive rules above, and that is what exams, publishers and style guides expect. When you enter a numeral, the converter checks it against those rules; if it is not standard it tells you why instead of guessing a value. A numeral that converts back to the same number is guaranteed to be in canonical form.
Numbers above 3,999

Because no letter is repeated more than three times, plain numerals stop at 3,999. For bigger values a horizontal bar over a numeral multiplies it by one thousand, so V̅ is 5,000 and M̅ is a million. The converter writes these with a combining overline character, which displays correctly in most modern fonts. For everyday use – years, chapters, events – you will rarely need them, but they are handy for puzzles and history lessons.

more: Why computers use binary and hex

Digital circuits have two stable states, so computers store everything as binary digits (bits). Long strings of ones and zeros are hard for humans, so we group them: three bits make one octal digit, four bits make one hexadecimal digit. That is why a byte (8 bits) is always exactly two hex digits, from 00 to FF, and why colours, MAC addresses and memory addresses are written in hex. Decimal remains the base people think in, which is why converting quickly between them matters.
Signed numbers and two’s complement

Computers store negative integers using two’s complement: invert all bits of the positive value and add one. In 8 bits, −1 becomes 11111111 (0xFF) and −128 becomes 10000000. The same bit pattern can therefore mean 255 or −1 depending on whether the type is unsigned or signed. When you choose a bit width the converter shows the stored pattern, its hex form, and how it reads as signed and unsigned, and warns you when a value does not fit in that width.
Converting by hand

To convert decimal to another base, divide repeatedly by the base and read the remainders from bottom to top: 13 ÷ 2 gives remainders 1, 0, 1, 1, so 13 = 1101 in binary. To go back, multiply each digit by the base raised to its position and add: 1×8 + 1×4 + 0×2 + 1×1 = 13. Hex works the same way with base 16, using A–F for 10–15. The tool does this instantly, but knowing the method helps you sanity-check results in exams and interviews.

more: What a Unix timestamp is

Unix time counts the seconds that have passed since the “epoch”, 00:00:00 UTC on 1 January 1970, ignoring leap seconds. Because it is a single number in UTC, it sorts correctly, is easy to compare and does not depend on anyone’s time zone or daylight saving. JavaScript and many modern APIs use milliseconds instead of seconds, so the same moment may appear as 1767225600 or 1767225600000. The converter recognises the scale by the number of digits.
Time zones and daylight saving

A timestamp is always UTC; the time zone only changes how it is displayed. Converting 1767225600 shows midnight on 1 January 2026 in London, 7 pm on 31 December in New York and 5:30 am in Mumbai. The tool uses your browser’s built-in time-zone database, so historical and future daylight-saving changes are applied correctly. When you type a date to convert into a timestamp, include an offset or “Z” if the source is not in your local zone.
The year 2038 problem

Older systems store Unix time as a signed 32-bit integer, which overflows at 03:14:07 UTC on 19 January 2038 (timestamp 2,147,483,647). After that, such systems wrap around to 1901. Modern operating systems, databases and languages use 64-bit time, which lasts for billions of years, but embedded devices and legacy file formats may still be affected. more: How the estimate works

The checker starts with the raw search space – the size of the character pool raised to the password’s length – and converts it to bits of entropy. It then subtracts strength for every predictable pattern it finds, because an attacker who tries common words and patterns first will reach your password much sooner than brute force would. The result is a cautious estimate rather than a guarantee: if anything, it errs on the side of calling a password weak.
Three attack scenarios

“Online” assumes someone guessing on a login page that limits attempts to about ten per second. “Slow hash” assumes a stolen database protected with bcrypt or a similar deliberately slow algorithm, at around ten thousand guesses per second. “Fast hash” assumes a leak stored with an outdated algorithm such as MD5 or unsalted SHA-1, attacked with graphics cards at a hundred billion guesses per second. A good password should survive the third scenario for centuries, because you can never be sure how a site stores it.

The key word is random: song lyrics, quotes and famous phrases are in attackers’ word lists. more: How the score is made

The calculator removes spaces, accents and punctuation, sorts the two names so their order does not matter, and runs them through a hashing function that turns any text into a number. That number is mapped to a percentage from 1 to 100 and a matching playful message. Nothing random is involved, which is why the result is repeatable – the fun is in trying different spellings and nicknames.
The FLAMES game

FLAMES is a pen-and-paper game played in schools around the world. Write both names, cross out the letters they share, and count the letters left. Then count around the word FLAMES by that number, crossing out the letter you land on each time, until one letter remains: Friends, Lovers, Affectionate, Marriage, Enemies or Siblings. The calculator plays it for you with exactly those traditional rules.
Real compatibility

Psychologists who study relationships point to things like shared values, good communication, trust, kindness and how couples handle conflict – none of which can be read from a name. Treat the score as a conversation starter, not advice. If a result makes someone feel bad, laugh it off and try their middle name; if you are thinking about a real relationship, talk to the person instead.

more: How the score is calculated

Typing tests use a standard “word” of five characters, including spaces and punctuation, so long and short words count fairly. Your net WPM is the number of correctly typed characters divided by five, divided by the minutes elapsed. Accuracy is the percentage of keystrokes that matched the text. Errors are shown in red as you type, and you can correct them – corrected characters count towards accuracy but not against your final speed.
Improving your speed

Touch typing – using all ten fingers without looking at the keys – is the single biggest improvement for most people. Begin slowly, focusing on correct finger placement from the home row, and accept a temporary drop in speed. After a few weeks of short daily practice, most learners overtake their old “hunt and peck” speed. Rhythm matters more than bursts: steady, even keystrokes reduce errors.
Choosing a test mode

Passages contain punctuation, capital letters and numbers, so they reflect real writing. Common-word drills use only frequent lower-case words, which is useful for building raw speed and finger memory. Custom text lets you practise exactly what you type at work – code, medical terms, another language. Compare scores only within the same mode, because punctuation-heavy text is naturally slower.
